Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 190, to amend the Exchequer Court Act.
He said: This bill is offering some slight amendments on matters of procedure. For instance, there are now two judges of the exchequer court, the chief justice and a puisne judge, and this bill is for the purpose of making it clear that either the president of the court or the puisne judge may exercise the power which in many statutes is conferred upon a judge of the exchequer court.
There is also a section of the act which provides that the practice and procedure in suits, actions and matters in the exchequer court shall be regulated by the practice and procedure in similar suits in His Majesty's high court of justice in England. That provision was made in 1877, and since then the practice and procedure in the high court of justice in England has been amended in many respects. Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve of the slavery convention signed at Geneva on the twenty-fifth of September, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-six, and which was signed, on behalf of Canada^ by the Canadian representative duly authorized to that effect;
And that this house do approve of same.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as the resolution indicates, this international convention was approved by the seventh assembly of the League of Nations. It was signed by the Right Hon. Sir George Foster, under authority of an order in council of Canada, passed on August 7th, 1926. The matter was fully discussed by the Assembly of the League of Nations, and Canada's representatives were present during the discussion. The convention contains twelve articles, which may be summarized as follows:
The contracting parties undertake to prevent and to suppress the slave trade and to bring about the complete abolition of slavery in all its forms. For this purpose they shall give to one another all possible assistance and undertake to prevent compulsory or forced labour from developing into conditions analogous to slavery. Disputes arising from this convention, if not settled by direct negotiations, shall be referred to the Permanent Court of International Justice or to some other court of arbitration.
Slavery is defined as being the status or condition of a person over whom any or all of the powers attaching to the right of ownership are exercised. The slave trade includes all acts involved in the capture, acquisition, or disposal of a person with intent to reduce him to slavery or with a view to selling or exchanging him and all acts of trade or transport in slaves.
The convention will come into operation for each state on the date of the deposit of its ratification or of its accession.
It is in order that the convention may be made applicable to Canada in this formal way that the present resolution is introduced.

speakeroldname: Hen. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot but feel that it is idle to ask this house to give its

Harbour Commissions
ratification and approval of any measure unless that measure has been printed and in the hands of hon. members for a sufficient time to enable them to study its provisions. We should be something better than mere rubber stamps in a matter of this kind. While the right hon. Prime Minister's explanation makes it abundantly clear that this is a convention to which parliament can give its assent, the fact remains that we should not be asked blindly to approve of any treaty without having had an opportunity to consider its terms and fully understand all its implications. At a later time I shall certainly avail myself of an opportunity to say something with respect to the whole procedure which is followed by this country in regard to the League of Nations, but this is not the time or place to speak of it. However, I do suggest to the Prime Minister that these treaties should be printed and in the hands of hon. members before they are asked to give their approval.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I hesitate to trouble the house
about a personal matter, but on March 29 last, during my absence from the house, in the course of a debate that arose on a motion of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland), the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) made certain observations which are reported in Hansard as follows:
Now is there no duty on the part of the government to See that the laws of this Dominion are carried out?
Whereupon the Solicitor General is reported to have remarked:
Before my hon. friend leaves Baldy Robb I would suggest, if he wants to know the reason, that he had better inquire of his own leader.
Whereupon the hon. member for West York replied:
That is a suggestion the hon. gentleman can safely make in the absence of my hon. leader.
The Solicitor General is then reported to have said:
I give you warning.
Subsequently, during a somewhat lengthy discussion towards the close of the debate, the Solicitor General stated that he withdrew nothing that he had said.
I regard these observations as very serious reflections upon myself. If I was in any shameful or discreditable manner associated with this convicted criminal, Baldy Robb, I

Privilege-Mr. Bennett
think I would merit the condemnation of the house. But the facts are these-and I ask my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) to follow me closely: Last summer, after the house had Tisen, I had occasion to visit the Minister of the Interior in his office at Ottawa in connection with a departmental matter. I do not charge my memory as to how exactly the circumstance arose, but during the course of the conversation something was said about Baldy Robb, and I thereupon observed that he had been released some time ago. The Minister of the Interior said that such was not the case-he had not been released-although as a matter -of fact a statement to that effect had appeared in the public press. It transpired that the minister was correct and we had some conversation touching the matter. My recollection is that I stated I would have nothing to do with it, pointing out, however, that I had recently been in Edmonton where I had learned that a large number of people there, who had been associated with the prosecution of Robb, were of the opinion that the ends of justice had been satisfied and the law vindicated by his conviction and imprisonment, and that, having regard to the fact that his wife and family were in poor circumstances, there was no reason why, if the government deemed it a proper course to pursue and such a recommendation should be made to His Excellency, Baldy Robb should not be released on ticket-of-leave. If I remember rightly the Minister of the Interior inquired whether I would have any objection to communicating that fact to the leader of the opposition. I told him I would not. I ascertained that the leader of the opposition was absent from Ottawa, as was also the Solicitor General, and I telephoned the Minister of the Interior to that effect.
I had no communication with the Solicitor General with respect to this matter. I made no recommendations of any kind regarding the release of this convicted criminal; I left the responsibility where it belonged. I did state, however, that I would not criticize any action that might be taken in the circumstances by the law officers of the crown. This view I intimated to the Minister of the Interior, the only minister with whom I had had any discussion with reference to the question. I desire to place this matter frankly before the House, without either comment or any endeavour to draw any inference from what transpired. I feel I owe this as a duty, primarily, not so much to myself as to those with whom I am associated in this house.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am sorry the Solicitor
General is not here; I know he would wish to say a word in reply to my hon. friend. But maj' I direct the hon. member's attention to a remark the Solicitor General made, which appears a little further on in Hansard, in which he makes it abundantly clear that he had no desire in any way, directly or indirectly, to imply that any action on the part of the hon. member was other than what everyone would wish and expect. The Solicitor General had been speaking of procedure in the remission of sentences and the propriety of discussing such matters on the floor of the house. But he made it perfectly clear that he imputed no improper motives to my hon. friend. Let me assure the hon. member, speaking not only for the Solicitor General but for every member of the government, that we all have that view and that view only.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
In connection with the release
of Baldy Robb I had received a very largely signed petition from the citizens of Edmonton and vicinity, inquiring whether, inasmuch as his wife was in delicate health and he himself was not in the best of health, and inasmuch also as all others who had participated in the wrongdoing had been released, it might not be possible to secure a remission of the sentence. Hence the discussion that took place between my hon. friend and myself. Apart from that discussion I know nothing about the matter. I conveyed the impression I received from the hon. member, which was that he would have no objection if the proper officers assumed the responsibility for releasing Baldy Robb.

National Battlefields Commission

Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 34, to amend an act respecting the National Battlefields at Quebec.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Payment of $750,000 authorized.
Will the minister kindly let us know first the sums we are now paying each year, and also what new work is proposed under the increased grant?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Very well. This explanation was given when the resolution was moved on February 10, but I will give it to my hon. friend again. Last year we paid a total of $75,000; in 1912-13 the amount was $116,500; the following year it was $145,000, and then $143,000. During the war period it ran from $34,000 to $52,000, while in 1926-27 the amount was $48,000. The commission point out that they can make their plans better by having a fixed amount for a period of ten years. The members of that commission are Sir George Garneau, Hon. A. Turgeon, Robert Bicker-dike, Senator T. Chapais, N. A. Dussault, Hon. W. H. Price, Hon. L. A. Taschereau, and Dr. A. G. Doughty.
My hon. friend has not told us the work which it is intended to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are numerous works and improvements contemplated; for instance, the Ross rifle factory is to be taken down and cleared away and other danger buildings around there are to be removed. That work ' is on capital account.
Are the Martello towers being looked after?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think they enter into this scheme.
How much has been expended to date by this commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They have expended each year the amounts which I have just given, totalling $1,078,010. That is what we have given them, and in addition to that I believe they have received some voluntary contributions.

Would the minister tell us what he expects this work to cost the country ultimately?
[The Chairman.]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will tell me how long the country will last I might give him an estimate. I am now giving what has been done since the first payment was made in 1912-13. Perhaps I had better read a letter which I recently received from the chairman of this commission under date of November 18, 1927, addressed to myself:
When I met you last in Ottawa, you asked me to remind you of the suggestion which I made to the subcommittee of the Privy Council in connection with the funds voted for the National Battlefields Commission.
At present, the ordinary expenses for administration and maintenance of the park amount to about $50,000 per year. It is estimated that when the park is finally completed the annual expense, for its administration and maintenance, will be about $75,000.
I suggested, and I strongly commend the idea to your favourable consideration, that instead of having parliament to vote the required grant each year it be given a statutory grant of $75,000. The excess of this amount over that required for maintenance will be applied to the work of completing the laying out and construction of the park (capital expenditure) and in course of time _ the maintenance will increase and the capital expenditure will diminish until we arrive at the estimated final cost of up-keep of $75,000 per year.
That is their estimate, and out of this amount we are now providing they will take care of capital expenditure.
Is there any revenue from it at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, it is a public park, the Plains of Abraham, as my hon. friend knows.

I do not think any man of business would do this; it is simply an invitation to reckless expenditure of public money. This is an admirable commission; it is doing excellent work, but when you place in their hands a given sum of money per annum you are simply inviting them to spend that amount, because human nature is only human nature. Would any corporation in the conduct of its business place in the hands of its directors a given sum per annum, regardless of their requirements, for the purpose of enabling them to carry on their work? This work should be budgetted; the requirements of this commission should be submitted to the minister yearly and these requirements should be carefully considered by the government and a sufficient sum placed in the estimates each year to meet them. The moment you do business this way, as I have said, you are simply inviting them to spend that much money. You may argue otherwise; you may remark how excellent is the commission, but my experience in business and elsewhere has been that where there is

National Battlefields Commission
a given sum of money available, human nature being what it is, that money is going to be spent by those who have control over it, and I therefore submit that the minister is wrong in adopting this method. I protest against placing a sum of money in the hands of any commission, amounting to $750,000 at the rate of $75,000 per year, by this method; if they have the money they will spend it. They are most admirable gentlemen, giving their services freely and gratuitiously for this work, but I submit that this is a wrong principle, because parliament is deprived of its power. Parliament now says, "Here is $75,000 a year for ten years; go and spend it." I protest against that method, having regard to the requirements of the public service at I know it elsewhere.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
On general principles no
person can find much fault with the observations of my hon. friend, but having looked into the matter after receiving the request from the commission for further sums of money to take care of the different buildings in that vicinity and to remove the Ross rifle factory, in addition to other work, we considered that it would be cheaper to say to the commission, "You cannot have any more money than this during the next ten years." They know they are going to receive this money each year and can plan their work accordingly, so I believe it will cost the treasury less in the end. In connection with keeping track of the expenditure, I would remind my hon. friend that under the Audit Act the Minister of Finance can send in auditors at any time, and as a matter of fact I believe they have already looked over these accounts.

Yes; I have looked over the accounts also.
Sir HENRY DiRAYTON:	Can my hon.
friend give us any real reason why an amount should not be voted each year in the ordinary way? I believe there has been no difficulty in the past in voting the money required.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Under the original act they
received an amount of $300,000; so money has been voted in this way before. The section of the act which is to be repealed authorized the payment of that amount to the commission.

I am only
speaking from memory, but I think my hon. friend will find that the $300,000 was voted for the initiation of the work and that sums of money have been voted each year since having regard on the one hand to what
parliament thought should be spent and on the other hand to the real requirements of the work. I think my hon. friend will find that in some years the vote was very small, while in other years the commission received much larger sums. For example, I think the vote has gone as high as $115,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The highest was $145,000.

And I think it has been as low as $34,000, so that each year it was a question of what parliament thought should be voted and for how much the work could be carried along. We got along pretty well in the past with that method; why not stay with it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Of course everybody
knows that this development must be completed. It is not only a national undertaking but it is an imperial undertaking. When the tercentenary of Quebec was celebrated there was a subscription not only in Canada but throughout the British Empire to buy the fields and the plains where the battles were fought which decided the fate of Canada in 1759; even school children in Canada and in the empire contributed for that purpose. The commission which was appointed to supervise the undertaking has done its work in the most admirable way. I am specially paying tribute to Sir George Gameau, the president of that commission, who has made it almost a personal affair, devoting most of his time to the work of the commission, trying to do that work as economically as possible, being there all the time, supervising everything, and giving his services freely.
Now there are some advantatges in the scheme proposed by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, and it is at the request of the commission that this change is being proposed. It is all very well to say that every year an amount may be voted in the estimates. Well I remember that a couple of years ago the Minister of Finance in his great zeal for and devotion to economy cut that item; Sir George Garneau threatened to resign because he could not go on with the work of the commission, and the minister had to reinsert the amount in the supplementary estimates.
Sir George Garneau and the commission are now proceeding to transfer the old buildings of the Ross Rifle Company, which are really an eyesore on the battlefield. They must be sure of a certain amount for a certain number of years. This method has been followed for a number of years in connection with other matters, for instance the contributions of this government to the highways

National Battlefields Commission
of the provinces. The provinces could rely upon a certain amount as a contribution to their highways for a certain number of years. Especially with the work which the commission has in view and the work which the commission has been doing, I believe this is certainly a reasonable demand, and that it should be granted.

Mr. Chairman, I just want to say one word in regard to this matter, not because of this resolution but because the same principle has been carried out, or is being carried out, in another place, and I do not think the principle is right. For instance, you have on this order paper, number 26, under the heading of the Federal District Commission, a certain amount of money-$250,000-set aside for sixteen years. Now we are asked to change that and vote that sum for thirty years, and I do not think that is right. It is a fact beyond question that during the years of the war and the years immediately succeeding the war there were many important and necessary public works which were necessarily held up. The government took the stand then, and very properly, I think, that not one dollar would be expended for this or that public building or public work where it was possible at all to get along without the expenditure, every dollar being required for war purposes, for the purpose of meeting the expenses of the war, and for several years thereafter.
Now it occurs to me that in connection with some of these large schemes of the government they are losing sight of the fact that for a number of years a great many works which should have been carried out have been held up.
I think the principle is wrong of voting a sum of money for a period of years without having placed before parliament at least a rough idea of what it is proposed to do with the money which is being handed over. That is the principle objection. I do not think anybody objects to the work that is going on in Quebec. I believe everybody is of one mind in regard to the fixing up of that place; it is historic, and it is something which belongs to all of Canada and which everybody in Canada would like to see in proper condition and maintained properly. I simply wish to register my objection as a general principle to the voting of sums of money for a long period of years. I do not think, having regard to the works which were held up for so many years, that it is just right at the present time.
fMr. Lapointe.]

I do not think the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) or the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) appreciates the point we are making, that here we are committing this country in future to these payments, whereas in other cases we are able to meet the annual demands from the resources we have in our hands from time to time. In the one case we pledge our credit and tie the hands of posterity. In the one case we make a direct and fixed charge upon the revenues, regardless of what they may be. In the other case, we contemplate just such an exigency as occurred during the war, when there was no longer money for such purposes and we had to curtail expenditures. I would like to ask my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior if he would not be as well justified in asking similar sums for Banff and Jasper. We base our expenditures upon our expected revenues, and a budget is for the purpose of endeavouring to have the expenditures met by the revenues, to provide sufficient revenues to meet contemplated expenditures.
The judges' salaries are a charge upon the revenue. The interest on the public debt is a charge upon the revenue. The payment of pensions is a charge upon the revenue, by statute. Now we are adding by statute two additional charges upon the revenue, regardless of what it may be, one in Quebec and one in Ottawa. The analogy in respect to highways does not apply. In connection with highways, the money was to be paid on condition that the province expended certain sums; and if conditions in this country warranted our being able to pay the money to the provinces, because they performed their duty under the statute and thereby earned it. It is only necessary to add that conditions, financial and otherwise, in the provinces would be reflected in the revenues of the Dominion; and if the provinces are able to make the expenditures, we would be able to implement our promise.
I would think this a grave departure from the principles that underlie parliamentary government. It is taking out of the hands of this parliament for a fixed determinate number of years an annual expenditure, regardless of what financial and other conditions in the country may be. This case is in Quebec; there is another in Ottawa; it will be in another case somewhere else; the principle involved will be endeavoured to be applied by people from every part of the country, and I am sure with an equal measure of justice. Under those circumstances we

Inspection oj Root Vegetables
can only record our protest against it, and add our tribute to what has been said by the Minister of Justice as to the work of this commission with Sir George Garneau at its head and which has become to him a labour of absorbing love. Perhaps no man has done more than he has in this matter. He says that this $75,000 is to take care of part of his capital expenditures; but he estimates that when all work is finished, the whole $75,000 will go for maintenance and expenses. However desirous we are to make this historic ground a park for all time, we should have regard to the great principle that governs appropriations of money for any public purpose, namely, that the budget should be submitted to the executive of the country and that the executive of the country should determine the extent to *which it will meet those demands and whether those demands should be met, having regard to the existing resources of the country and the effect which will be caused upon the revenues generally. That is the principle for which we contend and why w'e protest against this legislation.

Section agreed to.

Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior) moved the second reading of Bill No. 62, relating to the submission to parliament of certain regulations and orders in council.
Explain.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: In 1906 certain amendments were made to the acts mentioned in this bill and in addition there was a revision of the statutes. While the Department of the Interior has been tabling the regulations, action was not taken for complete validation by resolution of parliament, and therefore there is a doubt as to the validity of the regulations that have been passed since 1906, and by this bill we are seeking to validate all these orders in council that have been passed since that time.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: The principle involved is certainly unsound in part. Part of it may be sound, but certain people may have acquired rights; in fact, in one instance that I know of rights have been acquired. The people knew the order in council was invalid-they were so advised by their lawyers-and they acted accordingly. An order in council passed in January 1928, and not being validated by both houses of parliament before December 1929, there being an intervening session of parliament, would be invalid, and would have no force or effect at all, and therefore those who proceeded on the assumption of there being no order in council would be proceeding on sound ground. For us now to validate these orders in council en bloc, without having them before us at all, is most unsound, and I submit to the minister that if he is going to validate them, they should be attached to the bill as a schedule, or at least the orders in council should be laid on the table, because it is usual in a case of this character to protect the rights that have been acquired. There are not very many of them.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Oh yes.

There are; I had forgotten. The Minister of Justice will appreciate this point, that in law there are no orders in council at the moment. The period of time within which they might have been validated having expired, they have no longer any validity as orders in council, and not having validity as orders in council, peoples rights are not affected thereby. I do not say all of them: I am speaking of those that require validation by both houses of parliament, and which have not been validated at the next succeeding session of parliament. Their validity as orders in council has ceased; they are invalid; they are waste paper, and those who have acquired rights, being under the impression, the proper impression, that there was no valid order in council affecting the matter, may now be prejudicially affected by this legislation because it is retroactive in every sense of the term. It gives validity to something that has become invalid. It gives force to something that had no effect, and under those circumstances I ask the minister respectfully to submit to this house, or at least to lay upon the table, the orders in council in order that we may determine to what extent we may be interfering with the rights of people that may have accrued under and by virtue of the circumstances of there being no orders in council, by reason of the necessary action to validate them as provided by the statutes not having been taken.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: My hon. friend is quite correct up to a certain point, but whether his argument with respect to the omission to have validation annually by parliament carries full weight may be a question. However, I am free to say that the Justice department have advised us that there is that doubt, and they have advised this means of curing it, but we are not admitting even yet that the sanction of parliament is absolutely required to validate them. But I am frank to say that that is the advice we have been given by the Justice department. I am perfectly willing to table these orders in council, but may I say to my hon. friend that there is a great number of them dealing with regulations that have been passed from 1906 on, and it will be some, problem.
Some of them have been validated, I think.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
No, the officials of the department felt that their full duty was performed when these orders in council were tabled, but in the opinion of the Justice department apparently that was not

We have found ourselves in this position in the Yukon, that if we enforced that provision we would put some of the companies out of business. Therefore we have suspended the royalties in order to permit the companies to carry on, and I frankly confess that I do not like that system; I do not like recommending that responsibility to the government. I would much prefer the Ontario and Quebec system, under which the company has to earn a certain profit before a royalty is collected. I think we will all agree that unless a company is earning some profit it is not in a position to pay a royalty, and that is the reason I am asking for this change.

The hon.
member for Nipissing (Mr. Lapierre) interjected a remark a moment ago concerning which I would like to have some information. I would like to know if it is correct that

Yukon Quartz Mining Act

under Dominion government leases to-day a certain development is required within a certain period of time.

That is so under the
Ontario government.
I am talking about the federal act.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I would like to be definite about that; there are so many different leases.
Some of them contain that provision.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I know some of them do, but I do not want to make any mistake in answering that question. I will secure that information, however.

The minister has brought up a new point which seems to be very important; he says that unless a company is making a profit the government will not collect any royalty. Will he apply the same principle to the farmer with respect to the tariff? Is not that just as logical as the proposition which is now placed before us?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Unfortunately land has never been designated as a mineral, although I believe we are accused of mining the land out west. But land, whether profit has been made or not, has always been deemed to be taxable, whether in an urban or in a rural locality. That is the only answer I can make to my hon. friend. This, I must confess, is very much under the same principle as the income tax, and under the Income Tax Act no taxes are paid unless a certain percentage of profit is earned. In some degree it is a duplication of the income tax, and to that extent I think it is fair.

The Minister of the Interior has said that unless a company has made a profit they will pay no tax. It is quite true that land is altogether different from minerals; but on the other hand, whether the farmer makes a profit or not in any one year, he has to pay the tariff tax. speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is under a misapprehension. The company pays the provincial taxes and all other taxes of every kind. They are not exempt from taxes on their property; but when they come to pay royalty on their production, then insead of its being based on a definite amount per pound or per ounce, it is based on profits. That is all the difference.
That is my point as far as the tariff is concerned; if we do not make any profit we should not pay any tariff tax, and if we do make a profit we should pay the tax.

Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That the Militia Pension Act be amended,- 1. In regard to reservations from an officer's salary while in the public service of Canada: to the payment of a gratuity to a widow or children in case of death before pension may be granted; and to the payment of pensions to militiamen of His Majesty's army reserve who enlisted in the permanent force; and for additions to apply the Militia Pension Act to the royal Canadian navy and to that portion of the royal Canadian air force comprising solely the permanent active air force of Canada.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
Explain.

Two of the sections of the bill which is founded on this resolution are made necessary by the passing of the new Civil Service Superannuation Act and its substitution for the. Civil Service Retirement Act. In this respect the title of the new act is substituted for the old one. There is a section which provides for certain cases of hardship, in that widows and children do not receive any allowance where an officer dies before having served the requisite number of years required for pension. The Civil Service Superannuation Act provides that a gratuity, one month's pay for each year of service, is payable to the widows and children of civil servants who have not served full time for pension. Under this bill the provision is for the payment of the amount which has been actually deducted from the salary.

With or without interest?

Militia Pension Act

Without interest. There is also a provision to cover the cases of 149 men who were in the British army reserve. These cases were taken up before the commission with which I had something to do some years ago, and have been presented to this house from time to time. The situation was that certain men who had first served under the colours of the British army had then gone on the British army reserve and afterwards enlisted in the permanent force here. The condition of their enlistment in Canada was that they could be called up to the colours in the British army. The war came on and the Canadian authorities asked the British authorities to allow these men to serve here, which they did.

They having first been
called up.

A request having been
sent by the British authorities to the Canadian authorities asking that they be sent back, the Canadian authorities asked that they might be allowed to stay here. The British authorities consented that these men should be allowed to remain with the Canadian army, and they served with it. Their complaint is that by this action of the British authorities they were prevented from counting toward their service for pension their British service with the colours and in the reserve. Under the Militia Pension Act their service towards pension began to run only from the beginning of their Canadian service. It will be remembered, however, that the pay and allowance regulations of the Canadian service provided for a much higher remuneration than under British service, and also the rates of pension were very much higher. I think the view has been taken, although apparently no definite decision has been made, that possibly most of these reservists were as well off, in view of the higher rate of Canadian pension and the higher rate of pay, as if they had returned to the colours in Britain and served at the lower rate of pension and the lower rate of pay. However, it has been thought well to make an equitable adjustment of the matter, and the proposal of the bill will simply be this that these reservists be treated as if they had been permitted to go back to England when they were called up by the British authorities, and be paid by the Canadian authorities the amount of pension which they would have earned had they served with the British army during the war. Then if they 56103-1204
continued serving after the war their service counts towards pension period under the Canadian provision.
I should think that was not quite enough.

They have the option of accepting that plan, or of counting their full Canadian service towards a Canadian pension at the higher rate. I think this puts them in exactly the same position as if they had gone back and served in the British army.

Is that satisfactory to
the reservist?

I cannot say that. All
sorts of propositions have been made. I think it has even been proposed that they have both Canadian and British pensions.

How many will be affected
by this?

One hundred and fortynine, at the most; but many of these will find that settlement under Canadian regulations will be better than if they had gone back and taken the British settlement. There is another provision, and it is also rather technical, but it seems to be a case which should be provided for. In July, 1919, in order that a very large number of overseas officers might be discharged from the force on fair terms, an act was passed providing that when a man completed ten years' service he would be entitled to retire under pension; and under that act many officers who had served in the Canadian expeditionary force were discharged. It applied only to those of the permanent force serving at the time the act was passed. There were a certain number who served in the Canadian expeditionary force but who in July, 1919, at the time this act was passed, had been invalided out on account of wounds and who therefore did not come under the provision of the ten-year period. It has been thought fair to provide that the act of 1919, which permitted a man who had served overseas to have a pension on ten years' service, should apply to those who, by reason of wounds, were not actually in the service at the time. That provision is in this resolution. The last two provisions are to make the regulations of the Militia Pension Act apply mutatis mutandis to the Royal Canadian Navy and to that portion of the Royal Canadian Air Force comprising solely the permanent air force of Canada.

It is the intention of
the minister to send this legislation to the special committee?
Militia Pension Act

No, although I have no
objection whatever. This is a service pension, not a disability pension. It is in quite a different field and would involve an examination of an entirely different act from the one that the committee has been considering.

I think the option which the minister, on behalf of the people of Canada, is giving to reservists is very fair, but there is a tendency in all these pensions, under the Pension Act and in the pension committee, to gather everything and everybody within the folds of the act. If I am correctly informed, we have gathered into the act a lot of office boys, elevator boys who served as such during the war and who happened to be put into uniform, and I am credibly informed that a number of these are receiving larger pensions than the people who served over in France. I would suggest to the minister that he send this to the committee, and in order to be fair and just to everybody let us clean the whole situation up. There has been too much interweaving of the militia, the soldiers, the reservists, and practically everybody else in this country under the pension board, for the one purpose, of course, of getting a larger pension. The whole thing ought to be cleared up before the end of the session.

I understand my hon. friend's proposal, but I do not quite apprehend the reasons for it. In this resolution we are dealing with the Militia Pension Act, which provides for pensions for men who have given a certain amount of sendee in the militia. What my hon. friend is talking about is pensions to men who have suffered disabilities on account of war service. That is an entirely different thing and based on an entirely different principle. The one is to meet a lack of earning power caused by a disability incurred during the war, and the other is an award which is given to any public servant, either under the civil service or the army Pension Act or any other sort of superannuation act, after he has served a certain time, even though he is in full bodily health when discharged. Before thinking of referring this bill to the committee which has to do with returned soldiers' problems and pensions I should want to consult with the chairman of the committee. The pensions dealt with in that committee have to do with returned soldiers. It happens that these reservists who served in the war come in as well, not because of disability pensions but 'because of service pensions, and these reservists are asking for consideration because of British army service pension regulations, not as war pensions.
And some because the time limit and service wounds have put them out of pensions.

That is not brought in as a disability pension at all. As a matter of fact I do not think I have had any representation from any body of men with regard to that last class I mentioned; but men have been deprived of the benefit of the ten-year provision because -they happened to be discharged on account of wounds a little before that act -came into force. In this case again it is not a disability pension but a service pension which is granted.

Has the minister had any communication from officers now in our permanent service who claim that if this goes through they are not being fairly treated; in other words, that they have served in departments and are not getting the benefit of that service on joining the permanent force? Has the minister had any correspondence from any permanent officer in regard to cases of a similar nature to this?

I do not think I have with regard to a case of a similar nature to this. Many representations have been made in individual -cases by those who have felt that the disposition of their particular case regarding pension has not been just or equitable. I have endeavoured myself to review all those cases and to give every consideration to the representations made, bearing in mind that we have to have some sort of uniform system, and keeping in view the provisions in other acts as well. I think I can say that the bill founded upon this resolution is, generally speaking, a result of that consideration.

There is another class whose -case I have for some years been bringing to the attention not only of the present minister but of previous ministers. I refer to the case of service pensioners' wives and children who have been deserted and who are now living on charity and work, whereas the pensioner is in some other country enjoying a pension paid by this country. I have asked the minister for the last three years if some change could not be made so that the wife and children, living in Canada, of such pensioner should get the benefit of that pension.

My hon. friend has made representations, and exactly similar representations are made with regard to disability pensions. But it must be remembered that the pension is payable to the soldier, and it is very difficult for the pension authorities to enter the home and -determine the merits of a

Militia Pension Act
domestic dispute and legislate and say that the pension which is payable to the soldier shall be paid to somebody else. That is a matter for the civil, not for the pension authorities.

It is a very difficult one. The civil authorities cannot do anything about it. If the man is in the old country they cannot touch him. Month by month the pension is going out to that man, who may be living with another woman or under some unfavourable circumstances in another country, while the wife and children in Canada are without means of support. They cannot go to the Mothers' Allowance Board because they are met there with the statement: Go and find out where the man is and follow him with a civil action. There may be some legal reason why the Pension Act cannot be changed, but I do not know what it is. I think it is unfair to ask these people to take civil action.

Am I right in assuming that this legislation deals solely with the statutory right to pension based upon contributions made by the soldier or amounts withdrawn or withheld from his pay?
^Mr. RALSTON:	That depends upon
whether it is an officer or a non-commissioned officer or man. There are no deductions made from a non-commissioned officer or man as m the case of the officer.

This is an endeavour, then, to place the statutory pensions upon a little better basis. That is the whole story, as I understand it. There is one other point to which I should like to direct attention, and which has been touched on by the hon! members for Kingston City and Muskoka-Ontario. Not long since a case such as they mentioned came to my attention. I intended to write the department about it, but did not do so. It does occur to me that when this bill is being considered by the minister he might provide a section whereby, in the case of an order for support being made against the husband at the instance of the wife, the department would be enabled to pay the money to the wife. I think the minister could go that far. There are similar provisions in all the provinces dealing with the right of the wife to support by her husband, and if the department would take the same view that the Finance department took with regard to the Nova Scotia subsidies, when it withheld a portion of the subsidy because the province had not paid for troops that were sent down
there, I think an application of the same principle in this case might bring about the result we aim at.
What provision is made for the wives of non-commissioned officers and privates in case they get in distress?

I have not the act before me. There are a good many provisions in it but I think the act itself provides with regard to the widows of non-commissioned officers and men for gratuities, not for pensions. Pensions are based on the fact that contributions are made by officers. No contributions are made by non-commissioned officers and men. There is no change made by this act with regard to the wives of non-commissioned officers and men.
Is there any reason why they should not come in if they are willing to contribute?
It has never, I think,.been inquired into whether they are willing to contribute, but I should be very much surprised if they agreed to a contributory scheme.

Has the minister considered dependents other than the wife and children? I have a case in mind where
a military man left his sisters, who are dependent upon him, and who had contributed largely to the funds, and they have never been able to get anything in the way of a pension. To my mind their case is in the same category as those that have been referred to this afternoon.
I think my hon. friend has spoken to me about that case before. Was it the case of an officer who had not served the full period required for a pension?
I think he had served the full period.
There is no provision here for extending the ambit of dependants in that case. The dependants are the wife and children.

The minister referred in the course of his remarks to civil remedies where pensions were payable and the widow, or the grass widow, I should say, was not able to obtain a proportion of the pension. Is there any serious objection to providing legislation whereby if the wife is unjustly deserted she can obtain a proportion of the pension as a matter of principle?

I would say immediately that the pension paying authority would then be put in the place of a court trying a question
Militia Pension Act

of domestic relations between husband and wife. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition mentioned a different case, where an order had already been made and the matter dealt with by a court of competent jurisdiction.

The minister misunderstands me. I did not mean that the pension board should be placed in the position of a court, but was speaking of cases where there had been an order by the court. Let us say that the divorce court in Nova Scotia grants alimony. To-day the pension cannot be attached for alimony. I have one particular case in mind where the husband is looking forward to the divorce because he will get clear of supporting his wife, whereas a proportion of his pension is going to her so long as they remain married. If the court has made an order for alimony, is there any reason why the pension paying authority should not deduct the amount from the pension?
The same reason, I would think, why the employer of that husband should not be called upon to recognise an order for the payment of alimony.
You can garnishee his wages.

That is not simply recognising it and paying the amount without a special proceeding, and I do not think even a garnishee would apply until provision had been made so that the husband would be entitled to his maintenance. I shall be very glad to take the suggestion of the leader of the opposition into consideration, that is in cases where an order has actually "been made.
That is all I am asking.
My hon. friend said where the wife had been unjustly deserted.
I did not mean to say that, but I had in mind cases where there had been an order by the court, for alimony, for instance.
Is it clear, then, that the minister agrees that an order of the court shall be respected?

Will the minister
. agree to move that the committee rise so that he can consider this matter?
I think that is unusual.

I want to bring
before him the definite case of an officer.

That is all right. My
hon. friend can bring it up now.

There have been a number of cases where a soldier has died within two or three years after the war and left a widow, but she is not entitled under the law to receive a pension unless it can be demonstrated that the soldier's death was due to war service. Now' there are many instances where medical experts cannot positively testify that death was due to war service, and I therefore do not see anything unreasonable in my suggestion that if a soldier dies within a reasonable time, say within two or three years after returning from the war, his death should be considered due to war service. There is not a great number of these cases, and they should all be considered on the same plane. I know one or two cases where the widow is in difficulties because the husband died within a year or two-in one case within a year-after the war, and it was not clear that his death was due to war service. I think the country could well afford to regard these cases as being war casualties.

We all have cases similar to those to which my hon. friend refers, but they do not, I think, come within the spirit of the Militia Pension Act, which provides for pension only in the case of a definite period of service. What my hon. friend is referring to are cases which come under the Pension Act providing for pensions in case of death from war disability. Those are now being considered by the special committee, as my hon. friend knows.
It is being considered?

I do not know whether
the particular case which my hon. friend puts is being considered, but I shall be very much

surprised if it is not, because it was brought up whenever the problems affecting ex-service men are considered.

Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of National Revenue) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution.
That the Customs Act, chapter 42 of the revised statutes, 1927, be amended to make provision for a more adequate enforcement of the act and the prevention of smuggling operations in the territorial waters of Canada.
Explain.

The bill to be founded upon this resolution is the result of recommendations made by the royal commission with regard to smuggling, especially on the eastern coast of Canada. At all times there has been considerable doubt whether, in law, we have authority to make seizures within territorial waters of Canada beyond the three mile limit. The bill is intended to remove that doubt so far as it is possible to do so. With regard to vessels of British registry, we are extending the limit to twelve miles as well. There is also provision in the bill requiring importers to keep accurate and complete books of record of their importations. That has not been the case in the past, and in many instances it has been very difficult to establish that goods were smuggled.
That would not go far with bootleggers.

I am afraid not.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps
the minister will be good enough to explain to the committee the recommendations made by the royal commission that will not be included in the legislation under this resolution; or, if he desires it the other way, to explain which of the recommendations will find a lodging place in the statute that he now proposes to enact.

A very considerable number of the recommendations of the royal commission are embodied in three separate bills; one to amend the excise act, which has had a third
reading; another based on this resolution; and a third, the resolution for which will follow after this is disposed of.
This deals only with territorial waters?
That is all, except in regard to keeping complete books of record of importations.

Three or four years ago, Mr. Chairman, I brought this matter up in connection with the Bale de Chaleur. It has been the practice there for boats to stay outside the three mile limit and keep open bar both day and night, the fishermen getting their supplies of liquor from those boats and landing it at various points along the coast. The hon. Speaker co-operated with me in protesting against this practice, and asking for legislation to put a stop to it. I wish to congratulate the minister on this resolution, for I think no means would be too severe to put a stop to what has become a very serious abuse, leading to the demoralization of the fishermen and their families. I am sure the suggested legislation will meet with the hearty approval of people residing both in New Brunswick and Quebec.

It is in respect of that and similar matters that I am endeavouring to find out what the minister proposes to do. If my memory serves me correctly, His Lordship Bishop Ross wrote a letter to the royal commission in which he pointed out just what the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) has mentioned. At that time it was clear that we could not cope with the situation. Recommendations were made by the royal commission. Will the minister be good enough to explain just what he proposes to do to meet the situation? Owing to the shoal waters liquor boats anchored more than three miles from the shore of the Baie de Chaleur and the local fishermen sold their catch and with the proceeds bought strong drink, to the utter demoralization of themselves and the ruin of their families. It was felt at that time that we should consider the whole situation not only from the national, but possibly from the international standpoint also. Will the minister explain to the committee what is being done in that regard?

I regret Mr. Chairman, that I did not make myself clear on the point. As I said at the outset, there has been doubt whether we have power to seize any vessels beyond the three mile limit, although in what might be regarded as territorial waters of Canada. We want to be in a position to seize any vessel so long at is it in such waters.
i890
Customs Act
What is the definition of territorial waters?

I do not know. I am free to admit that a difficulty may be encountered there, and the question is one that must be left to the judgment of the courts. They must say what constitutes territorial waters. I do not think anyone can say absolutely, with regard to any particular section of the coast, what comprises the territorial waters of Canada and what does not.
Will this apply to other than British vessels?

If in territorial waters of
Canada, yes. AVith regard to Canadian vessels or vessels of British register there will be a limit of twelve miles from our own coast.

Twelve miles off Halifax,
say?
Yes.
Where under heaven can you get a power like that?
They are our own vessels.
But they are outside your own territorial waters.
This is entirely in harmony with the recommendation of a commission consisting of three judges. I do not know whether my hon. friend has any confidence in their opinion.
I have not the slightest confidence in it if it applies to vessels twelve miles off Halifax. The Supreme Court of Nova Scotia in a case tried recently decided otherwise.
My hon. friend will not say that this will do any harm?
I fancy you will find yourself in a blind alley; you will get nowhere. The courts will hold such a provision as this ultra vires.
Why twelve miles?
Because the United States fixed upon that limit.
For that matter, why three miles?

That limit is for international
purposes.
Well, we might have made it thirteen. As a matter of fact we thought of making it eighteen, but it was felt that twelve miles would be a fair range.
I presume that what the minister is really doing is following the tentative arrangement made between Great Britain and the United States?
Yes.

And that gives a right of search up to twelve miles; that is my recollection. With regard to the three mile limit, the minister professes ignorance of the reason for that arbitrary limitation having been established. Surely he must know what that reason was. Every country has the right to protect its coast, and three miles was fixed upon for the reason that, at the time that limitation was established, three miles was the range of cannon. One argument advanced by the United States in relation to the twelve mile limit was that the range of shore cannon had tremendously increased, and they felt that the limit should be correspondingly extended. At any rate, whether right or wrong, the three mile limit was fixed for the reason I have stated. But my hon. friend has not answered this pertinent question: What are territorial waters so far as Canada is concerned? The minister confesses that he is unable to answer the question, and I sympathize with him in his view that the question is one for the Justice department. But has not the Minister of Justice been taken into my hon. friend's confidence in connection with the bill? I speak subject to correction, because I have been away so much, but I remember that in connection with the customs investigation Mr. O'Connor was consistently of the view that most of these waters were enclosed to us-mare clausum, over which we had sovereign rights. He thought the Bale de Chaleur was one of these, as well as the Northumberland straits. He prepared an argument in support of this view-an argument for which, by the way, he was not paid. Nor was he allowed to sue for payment. Is the minister adopting Mr. O'Connor's opinion without having paid him for it? At any rate, I think seriously we are entitled to know exactly what we are doing. Take for example lake Ontario, Where there is considerable activity: I am sure the minister desires to take action there. Well, is that a territorial water of Canada?
I think it would be, to the middle of the lake.

Is that understood with the United States in connection with the endeavour to put a stop to the nefarious practice there?

Customs Act
This is not particularly designed for the lakes; the legislation is intended to apply to the coasts.
Has the minister any definition of "territorial waters"? Is there any such definition in the bill?

No, but I may say for the benefit of my hon. friend that the bill has passed the scrutiny and had the approval of the Department of Justice. I am not a legal man and candidly I do not know what might constitute territorial waters in any given case. Would my hon. friends tell us where, in their opinion, territorial water begins or ends at the mouth of the St. Lawrence, for example? Can that be decided? We must take each case as we come to it.

I do not propose to answer the minister's question, but I ask him in all seriousness to tell us just what the purpose of this bill is. Is it intended to justify or to attempt to justify seizures beyond three miles from low water wark on the coast line, say, of Nova Scotia?
If they are hanging about the coast outside the three mile limit and we know that their object is to smuggle, we want to be able to seize them.

Regardless of the flag
they fly?
If within territorial waters, yes.

But what does the minister mean by "territorial waters?" The definition given in the British Territorial Waters Jurisdiction Act is, three miles from low water mark; so that within a radius of three miles around an island a ship would be within territorial waters.
That is not in accordance with the argument of my hon, friend from West York.

It is in accordance with the findings of the court. In the case of Mason versus Coffin, in which the department made a seizure beyond the three mile limit, the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia only a few months ago held this action to have been unwarranted. It is therefore futile to pass such a law. Why does not the minister go to the British parliament and have the Territorial Waters Jurisdiction Act enlarged if he feels that the present law is not wide enough? We have no constitutional power in the matter, and if the minister is honest he will appeal to
the British parliament to have the law amended. I should like to see this done, but the minister should recognize that this parliament has not the power to pass such a law as this.

Any improvements in the customs regulations will be in the public interest. This whole question dates back to the pioneer work done in this house by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), who was mainly responsible for the collection of $60,000,000 of customs dues which otherwise would not have been received. Has the minister endeavoured to enforce our customs regulations without seeking help from the admiralty of the United States? I noticed the other day that an armed flotilla of American boats entered the port of Walker-ville, within the territorial waters of Canada, over the head of the Canadian government, and fired off guns and rifles, breaking windows, according to dispatches in various papers in the Toronto district. If the government of Canada need life-saving operations carried out on the great lakes they must at present appeal to American life-saving stations. When there is a mine disaster and 100 men or thereabouts are killed or injured, as in the case of the Hollinger mine, they have to go to Pittsburgh to get a life-saving crew. Is the government going to depend upon the United States in order to prevent smuggling in territorial waters of Canada, and appeal for assistance from American customs boats? How much longer is the government going to stand for that sort of thing? It is all very well to say that they are tightening up the regulations, but the fact is that around Windsor and elsewhere they have to rely somewhat on American craft to-help them enforce their regulations. Where is this wonderful external affairs department with, its admiralty. Where is the admiral, with an American invasion at Walkerville? I hope the minister will become active. I must give him credit for having been active in the past year and having tightened up the regulations, on the initiative of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. But these regulations should be enforced without help from the admiralty of the United States. I hope now that this wonderful Department of External Affairs will get busy and mobilize our fleet in the Detroit river to protect the citizens of this country instead of sending ambassadors all over the seven seas. Smuggling should be prevented by co-operation between the two governments, and we should tell the authorities of the United States that when they cross into Canadian waters they are in a dangerous position, without regard to our new status.
Customs Act

I have no knowledge whatever of American preventive officers or boats entering Canadian waters and firing shots on Canadian ports. The house in committee on Bill No. 43, respecting the Bell Telephone Company of Canada-Mr.	Edwards	(Ottawa)-Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Power to increase capital.

I have given notice of an amendment to this bill, Mr. Chairman. It is now twenty minutes past eight, and I intend to talk until nine o'clock. I am surprised that this proposal of the Bell Telephone Company to increase its capital stock from $75,000,000 to $150,000,000 should meet with no protest from the committee or from this house, and particularly from the Progressives, who are supposed to be adherents of the principle of public ownership. This company is nothing but an American monopoly, which has crossed the border into Canada. It first came to parliament in 1880 and got its incorporation, under chapter 67. It came back again in 1882, and asked for amendments which were incorporated in chapter 95; in 1884 it came back again for further amendments, chapter 88; in 1892 it came back again and got further amendments, chapter 67; in 1894 it applied for further amendments, which were incorporated in chapter 108; in 1902, chapter 41, it applied for an increase in its capital stock; it came back again in 1906, and got another hand-out from this parliament, by chapter 61; in 1920, which was the last time we saw them around this chamber, by chapter 100 the company was practically given the title deeds to the country and granted a monopoly throughout the whole of Canada. As a result what happened? In the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba they established government owned telephone systems in order to be free of this masterful American monopoly. The late Sir Adam Beck proposed that the province of Ontario should establish a government owned telephone system, but corporation activity killed the proposal.
There is practically no regulation of the Bell Telephone Company. Almost every rate application that has been made by the company to the Board of Railway Commissioners has been granted in toto. The company is a law unto itself; it is supposed to own the heavens above, the earth beneath, and the waters under the earth. When the municipalities applied to the railway commission to remove the discrimination in telephone rates the commission decline to hear oral argument and told counsel to file written argument-which no doubt was put in the wastepaper basket by the so-called rate regulators. In brief, you might just as well abolish the railway act so far as effective control of this corporation is concerned and go back to the old law of supply and demand as a rate regulator.
In 1917 the Drayton-Acworth report recommended that before any applications for in-
Bell Telephone Company

creased rates were granted by parliament they should be reported on by the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada. Why was not that course taken in this case? Why should this company be singled out for favoured treatment? The Northern Electric Company is part and parcel of the Bell company. The Northern company has practically a monopoly in the supply of telephone apparatus and there is no regulation of its charges to the parent company. In fact, the Board of Railway Commissioners found that the Northern Electric Company was outside their jurisdiction and could not be required to submit its records for inspection in connection with the recent application of the Bell company for increased rates. The hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary) has introduced a bill this session to amend the railway act in relation to the investigation of subsidiaries of telephone or telegraph companies like the Northern Electric, and I submit that it should be passed before one line of this bill is adopted. For the information of the house let me quote from that bill:
"1. Section three hundred and seventy-five of the Railway Act, chapter one hundred and seventy of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, is amended by inserting the following subsection immediately after subsection twelve thereof:-
"(13) The board shall have jurisdiction to inquire into and investigate the affairs of any company, corporation of firm in which any telephone company or telegraph company subject to the jurisdiction of the board has, in the opinion of the board, a controlling interest as shareholders or partners, or of which such company, corporation or firm in the opinion of the board is a subsidiary, and to examine the books, accounts, vouchers and papers of the said company, corporation or firm, and for such purposes and to that extent the said company, corporation or firm shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the board."
In my opinion the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) ought to take over the hon. member's bill, because unless it is treated as a government measure there is very little prospect of its being enacted this session. I hope that before this $75,000,000 hand out to the Bell company is granted the hon. member for South Toronto will insist that his bill become law in order to confer on the Board of Railway Commissioners jurisdiction over such a company as the Northern Electric, which is purely a subsidiary of the Bell company, formed for the purpose of supplying to the parent company telephone apparatus at fabulous prices.
The government of Ontario opposed the application of the Bell Telephone company for increase of rates to which I have already referred. They were represented before the 
railway commission by Mr. Reid, who did well there, and he has since seen fit to write a letter to that public ownership organ, the Toronto Globe. The Globe up to a few years ago was always considered to be the mouthpiece of the Liberal party, but latterly it has been somewhat critical in its attitude towards its old-time friends. It was not the Globe that deserted the Liberal party; the Liberal party deserted Liberal principles and the Globe upheld Liberalism. The Globe is a supporter of public ownership of public utilities. I am interested in the attitude of the Liberal party towards this bill. In the late election our opponents went up and down the country charging that the Conservative party was the party of the "big interests." Where is the Liberal party to-night regarding this bill? In the railway committee did the government voice any opposition to this obnoxious measure? Did the government lay down any policy for such a hand out as this -an increase in capital from $75,000,000 to $150,000,000 by this company, with scarcely a tittle of evidence presented to the committee as to any necessity for the increase? I am not here to attack this or any other public utility. I have considerable sympathy for most of our public utility companies, for they are having a hard time to make ends meet in face of the heavy increase in taxation and the greatly enhanced cost of labour and materials; but I do say that before any such increase as is proposed by this bill is granted there should be a thorough and impartial investigation of the Bell Telephone Company and of the subsidiary Northern Electric Company by the railway commission as to the necessity for this particular increase of capital. What do they propose to do with this extra $75,000,000? Does anyone argue that if this bill passes to-night the Bell Telephone Company will devote this money to extensions? No. I venture to say that from $25,000,000 to $50,000,000 of it will be a split of common stock or just a melon to be cut up among the shareholders, paying dividends running up to $50,000,000 on all classes of stock issued, with the result that the telephone users will have to shoulder an added burden in rates on this watered stock. In the hydro-electric system the rates are based upon the actual investment in the enterprise; but when people in the cities buy, say, a quart of milk or a loaf of bread they pay not only the actual worth of that milk and bread, but also extra millions in rates represented in dividends paid out on the various common stocks of no par value.

Bell Telephone Company
I venture to say that when this stock is issued and placed on the market a large block of it, anywhere from ten to forty million dollars, will be common stock which will represent not a dollar put into the undertaking. The telephone users of the country will pay for it. In the past two years an application has been made to the Board of Railway Commissioners by this company for an increase in rates. The municipalities appealed to the Board of Railway Commissioners asking to have removed this unfair and altogether unjust discrimination. But what does the government of Canada do? Through the national railways the government entered into a private contract over the heads of the commission whereby the government and the national railways get certain cut rates from the Bell Telephone Company at the expense of the rest of Canada. The government itself, for its own purposes, made that private arrangement with the company for the reduction of rates, with the result that telephone users in Ontario and Quebec, through the discrimination which the company showed in favour of the government on the one hand and the Canadian National Railways on the other, were compelled to shoulder an unwarranted burden. The people of this country expect, if public rights are to be respected in this parliament, that some brakes shall be put on this monoply. AVith the sanction and approval of the Dominion government and by order of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, the telephone rates of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada were recently increased all over the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and a new and additional burden of taxation was thereby imposed upon all of these telephone users of over $2,600,000 per year.

This is not an ordinary matter of business at all; it is not any question of having time within which to get in your profits and look after your business and all that sort of thing. My friend has not yet grasped the point. As soon as the money is in the hands of the manufacturer it belongs to this country; that is the point. What happened during the days when I knew a little more about these things than I do at the moment? There was one firm in Toronto, for instance, which owed this country vast
Special War Revenue Act

sums of money. I am not sure that it has not since gone into liquidation. Had there been an efficient and effective control over that matter, that condition could not have arisen, because it was a business in which they got their money right at once. I do not want to mention their business. It was practically a cash business-cash within thirty days; they got that money from their customers, and, as the minister says, they set up their reserves and that kind of thing; then when the time came that the government wanted their money, the company wapted it in their business. The way to deal with such a case is in the summary method which is at least two hundred years old, by the issue of a writ of sequestration. The Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) will remember that in New Brunswick the writ of sequestration was applied. I was a young man then and acted for the government there. The same principle could be applied here, the writ of execution where the minister is satisfied that the money has come into the hands of the company. I do not like this matter of paying five or six hundred lawyers. You recognize that lawyers all over the country are employed if they are favoured. If my information is correct, there are a vast number who should be sued, but who are not.
