DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT

speechtext:
Hon. J. H. KING (Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That the Department of Health and of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment be amalgamated in a single department to be called the Department of National Health and Veterans' Welfare, presided over by a minister of the crown; that the powers and duties of the minister be defined; and provision be made for the appointment of a deputy minister, the making of regulations, and the employment of such other officers, clerks, and employees as may be deemed necessary.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext: I think the minister might make some explanation. I would like to know what the idea really is. We now have a committee with very wide powers inquiring into what ought to be done in the interests of the soldiers. Has the minister considered having this question dealt with by that committee? The soldiers' re-establishment is a long way off from being completed. It might be well for the minister to consider the advisability of getting whatever light he can on this subject from that committee, which is now functioning.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext:
The resolution is along the line of the suggestion by His Excellency on the opening of the session, that the departments of Health and of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment be amalgamated into a single department to be known as the Department of National Health and Veterans' Welfare. The Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment came into being in 1918, with a view to assisting the men who were then returning from overseas to re-establish themselves in civil life. Shortly after the war ended the department absorbed the Military Hospitals Commission and took over its functions. A little later they took over largely the staff of the Pension board and have been functioning accordingly. The experience of the last few years would indicate that the work of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment to-dary is to a great extent that of health activities in reference to those men who were disabled overseas. It is true there is still some work being carried on in the matter of re-establishment. It is proposed by this amalgamation to maintain for a time at least

National Health and Veterans' Welfare
the veterans' bureau as a unit within the Health department, and the work will be continued probably along the lines followed from its beginning. The work of re-establishment, the work of administration as far as the Pension board is concerned, and the treatment of the vet shops, which as a matter of fact is health work, will be continued in the veterans' welfare bureau. As far as the bill itself is concerned, if when it reaches the second reading it is the view of the house that the matter is of such a character that it should be referred to the committee now dealing with soldier matters, I shall be very glad to accept that suggestion and have it so referred.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext: I would like to ask the minister the reason for the word "national" coming into the name, and why change the name from "Soldiers' Re-establishment" to "Veterans' Welfare"?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext: I think my previous remarks dealt with re-establishment. As a matter of fact the department to-day is really a welfare department dealing with pensions, hospitalization and vetcraft work, which is a form of treatment, and some consideration was given to the question of changing the title. In amalgamating the two departments we felt that if we could call the new department the Department of National Health and Veterans' Welfare, that would probably meet with the view of parliament and also of the country generally.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext:
Does the minister not
think that the term "Veterans' Welfare" might imply some sort of charitable organization? Would it not be better to have such a name as "Soldiers' Affairs," or something more proper and dignified and indicating in a better way the real purpose of the department? After all, the department will have to carry on a good deal of work which is not really welfare work as that is understood. The term "welfare" has a popular meaning, and it seems to me both undignified and hardly applicable to the business which the government has to do with respect to ex-service men and soldiers generally. It would be far better to use a name such as-and this has just come to my mind offhand-Department of National Health and Soldiers' Affairs, or Department of Health and Soldiers' Affairs. I think the minister will find, when he gets his bill through and the measure comes before the public, that the name "Veterans' Welfare" is not as appropriate as some others.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext:
I concur entirely in the
view of the hon. member for Vancouver
South, except possibly as regards the name "Soldiers' Affairs." I see no reason for changing the present name.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext: I concur in that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext: I understand this department will still embrace pensions?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext: How is that veterans' welfare? It is not a dignified name. The designation should remain as it was, because "Department of Health and Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment" is a dignified name and one generally understood by the country. I see no reason for inserting the word "national". After all no one can have any doubt that the Department of Health refers to the health of the nation. Why not insert the word "National" before "Finance", before "Trade and Commerce", before "Agriculture"? For instance, why not have the "Department of National Interior"? We might just as well have National Secretary of State and so on, as the Department of National Health. There is no distinction whatever. This department obviously applies to the health of the nation and the word "national" is superfluous. To change the name from "Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment" to "Veterans' Welfare" would not be of any assistance in dealing with soldiers' problems. The old name is one recognized by the soldiers generally and it should not be changed to a name which, as my hon. friend has just said, implies something in the nature of charity.	[DOT]

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext:
It does not. I
think it is important to adopt the designation, "Department of National Health," because we have provincial health departments in every province. It could be called the Dominion Health Department or the National Health Department. It is different from the Interior department and other departments of government and I think the change is warranted. I cannot see any great advantage to anyone in continuing the term "Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment", which is a long, cumbersome name, and one which does not to-day represent the activities of the department, because, as I have said, the major activities are not those of re-establishment. The name does not matter so much. The proposed name has been before the public for some months now and I have not heard through the press or correspondence any objection to the term "Veterans' Welfare." It should not be intimated for a
1910	COMMONS
National Health and Veterans' Welfare
moment that that name would indicate the setting up of a charity department. That is not the intention.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext:
Have the public really
been apprised of the term "Veteran's Welfare?" I for my part did not know of it until I heard it to-night, and I think ninety-nine per cent of the people do not know of it.

Is there any objection to

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext:
This amalgamation is not in the public interest. It will work out as a department of all health and no soldier. The public is disappointed at the way in which the soldier has been bandied about by this government. He was first tacked on to the Department of Militia. Then the government made a football of him, creating a new department, a Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment. Sometimes the minister of that department was here; sometimes he was an absentee landlord. Now it is proposed to have a health department and to tack the soldier on to that. The government are making a political football out of him, and no economy will be effected by the proposed change. If there is to be a department it should be a department of returned soldiers. The returned soldier has not been treated as he should have been by the various governments that have represented the people of Canada. It takes months and months to get a soldier into a hospital. Some time ago I sent forward a letter from the Reverend Canon Skey, one of the leading Anglican rectors in the diocese of Toronto, requesting that some poor returned soldier who was out of his mind should be put in the Christie street hospital in my constituency. This man's wife had to go out to work. After the home had been visited on several occasions by the canon and others, it was felt that the returned soldier, who was 
suffering in body and mind as a result of the war, should be in the Christie street hospital. I wrote to the minister, but he was out of town. I wrote to the deputy and I received a reply that I could apply to the Board of Pension Commissioners, or some other high court of justice, or the privy council perhaps, and all that red tape before anyone had any power to take any action. We have to-day a proposed amalgamation. It seems that the returned soldier is the only agency to which the government will apply economy, although they are spending money like water in the Department of Public Works. Along the St. Lawrence river you can see a wharf almost every mile, and if anybody has not got a wharf in Ontario and Quebec he must have been derelict in his duty; but when it comes to effecting economies, the economy is always against the poor returned soldier. This wonderful Department of Health which is to be amalgamated with Soldiers Civil Re-establishment, what does it do? As a matter of fact most of the health work is done by the municipalities and by the provincial governments. It is they who maintain the hospitals, and when an epidemic comes along this government gets off scot-free and the work is shunted off on to the provinces and the .municipalities. In the city of Toronto there are thousands of returned soldiers out of work, and they are going in hundreds across to the United States, having been driven out of Canada by the economic and soldier policy of this government. In my constituency and in every constituency in Toronto a soldier has to pay a dollar and join the Liberal ward association to get a job even as a temporary clerk in the post office at Christmas. Now these departments are to be amalgamated under the high sounding name of National Health and Veterans' Welfare. In my opinion this new department is nothing but camouflage, but let me tell the minister that you can fool the returned soldiers no longer. The returned soldier is becoming sick and tired of being bandied about by this government from the customs to the post office from the Department of Soldiers Civil Re-establishment to the Civil Service Commission, and having to pay a dollar and join the ward association in order to get a temporary job at Christmas. A returned soldier could not be employed in the Toronto post office at Christmas unless through a Liberal patronage committee.
The returned soldier is made a political football of in Canada, and if there is one class of people for whom a separate department should be created and maintained, no matter what the cost, it is the returned soldier. But

National Health and Veterans' Welfare
he is the only person the government economises against to-day, at the expense of his health, at the expense of having no grave in which to rest his bones in the cemetery unless he pays a dollar and joins the ward association.
There will be no economy effected by this amalgamation. This new department is to be presided over by a minister of the crown, and no doubt it will be a nice easy department to preside over. All the minister will have to do is to attend the sittings of parliament, and then take a trip home, and let the deputy minister and the assistant deputy and a great retinue of officers and clerks carry on in the recess at the expense of the returned soldier. There will be an absentee landlord presiding over this high sounding amalgamation and conglomeration. Good-by and good night to the returned soldier if anything will be accomplished in his interests by such an innovation as this. No doubt under this new department the returned soldier 'will continue to get all the pick and shovel jobs, for that seems to be the favourite job which is handed out to the returned soldier, but when it comes to appointing someone to the senate, what a difference! Some young gentleman who served in the ward associations and not in the war is given the preference, and it is the same with appointments of judges. You talk about increasing the salaries of judges, but I ask what about giving some greater measure of compensation to those who risked their lives for the benefit of Canada and are now suffering in the poorhouses in the city from which I come, where they have to pass the hat around and hold tag days to get enough money to tide the returned soldiers over the winter months of the year.
Here we are considering a resolution to amalgamate the Department of Health with the Soldiers Civil Re-establishment into one single department, no doubt with a single object

to wipe the returned soldier off the map altogether. We can spend two and a half millions for the care of cattle, and millions more to put down bug and insect pests and hog cholera, but not a five dollar bill when a soldier gets sick. He goes to the hospital and cannot get medical treatment. I know dozens of men who have been turned away from the hospitals. I wrote to the chairman of the committee on pensions-I wish they were all as good as he is-regarding a deputation that was ready to come down from the city of Toronto, and I was told that the committee had no time to consider their memorandum of complaints which had been sent on to me as the representative of this soldier constituency of Toronto Northwest,
which includes the Christie street hospital, asking for reforms at the hands of this parliament. The committee had no time to consider their memorandum, but we have lots of time to discuss an amalgamation that, so far as the returned soldier is concerned, will not amount to anything, and you might just as well let him depend on charity, as he has to do very largely in the district from which I come. In the city of Toronto they have had to open soup kitchens for the unemployed and appeals are being made by different missions, including the Revillie one, which are seeking money from the business men in order to provide the returned soldier with a loaf of bread and clothing to cover his body over the winter months. On the front page of a recent edition of a Toronto paper you will see an appeal signed by the secretary of one of these societies and the Poppy day Committee asking that cast off clothing be sent to such and such an office, because there are many children of returned soldiers who have not enough clothing. If there is one department that should be a department by itself, presided over by an active minister who will give all his time to the work, it should be a department that will look after the welfare of the soldiers from coast to coast. They are dying off by hundreds and thousands every year, and the economic policy that is being followed by this government is depriving them not only of a living but of a pension as well. I was told by some of the Toronto university graduates who have just returned from the Olympic games that there is hardly anybody in Germany out of work. While we are talking about peace resolutions and all of that, Germany is taking care of her veterans. In Germany the veteran does not need to work at all. Doctor Hudson, a very fine young doctor of the Varsity team, told me he talked with many men in the city of Berlin, and they told him that their soldier policy was this, that all the veterans who fought in the late war were retired on a pension. The ablebodied young men are given employment under an arrangement by which in the event of trouble they are to be ready to enlist and go to the front again, but the veterans get a pension equal to their civil pay. In Canada from 25 to 30 per cent of our returned soldiers get no pension at all. Many of them are not 100 per cent efficient and cannot get work. They are out of work to-day in the Toronto district through no fault of their own. I protest against such economy. I say it is false economy, and the public do not ask for that kind of economy. If there is one place where economy is being practiced by this govern-
1912	COMMONS
National Health and Veterans' Weljare
ment to-day, it is against the returned soldier. In my opinion the health department should be an active department by itself. This country with only one-eleventh the population of the United States has about seventeen government departments as against seven or eight active departments in the republic. I wish to protest against this amalgamation. It is not in the public interest, and first and last it is not in the interest of the returned men.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext:
There is no one in the house who has a W'armer spot in his heart for the returned men than I have, and I may be permitted to answer my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Church). The returned soldiers' committee of which I am proud to be a member is sitting on the cases of returned soldiers, and, irrespective of party, the members of that committee are endeavouring to bring in a report that will in every respect do full justice to our returned men. When we have brought in our recommendations, should the government see fit to reject them, then would be the time to condemn them in the terms which my hon. friend has employed; but until that time arrives and we have fully considered what shall be done in justice to our returned soldiers, I think such condemnation is premature.
In my opinion the title "Veterans' Welfare " savours too much of charity. Only today I received a letter from the city of Calgary asking for a small contribution to the Board of Public Welfare, which deals with charitable cases. Perhaps the returned men themselves might be able to suggest a better name. At any rate for the time being I would suggest to the minister that the title be held in abeyance until a more suitable name is forthcoming. As regards the other portion of the title of the proposed amalgamation, " National Health ", I think it is wisely chosen, because there are already provincial departments of health.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext:
I wish to support what has been said by hon. members with regard to a change of the proposed title. I do not see any advantage in the word "National"; I think it is superfluous. In my opinion the title might very well be cut down to "Department of Health and Soldiers' Re-establishment." This title would be appropriate to the two branches forming the amalgamation, and would be recognized by the soldiers themselves as a continuation of the department that has carried on in the past. I am disappointed in one feature of this proposal- it does not bring about any economy. Some time ago I pointed out that there was an in-

creased expenditure in the two departments of some $35,000 although they are under one minister. I presumed they were united for purposes of economy, but, as is so characteristic with this government, no economy of management has resulted so far. I think the minister should decide without further discussion to pass the whole matter over to the committee dealing with returned soldiers' problems so that it may be fully considered by them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext: Has any demand been made by the returned men's association for this change of title to "Veterans' Welfare"? I would suggest to the minister that the soldiers' branch of the amalgamated department being the most important, if the present title must be changed the new united department should be termed " Department of Soldiers' Re-establishment and Health."

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext:
I am desirous of
getting a name that will be appropriate to a department of the character now proposed. I notice that in 1918, when Sir Robert Borden introduced the measure to bring into being the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment, he stated that within a reasonable number of years it would probably go out of existence altogether. There is a feeling that we have arrived at the stage where this department could be amalgamated with the Department of Health and the two departments thus made more helpful to the whole organization. I suggest that the resolution be allowed to carry, and when the bill based thereon reaches second reading we can discuss the title and other matters pertaining to the amalgamation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext:
That is distinctly on the
understanding that the name which appears in the resolution will be open to discussion?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext:
I think there is
something altogether wrong in this resolution, because this is not a department of national health; that is, it cannot interfere in any way with provincial jurisdiction.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext: It covers national health matters, that is all.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext:
Will the minister
explain how he could have interfered in the recent typhoid epidemic in Montreal, which was a menace to the health of the whole Dominion? I agree that there should be a federal health department, and if it is possible so to constitute it without interfering with provincial jurisdiction, I am agreeable to its

National Health and Veterans' Welfare
formation; but I fail to see how it can be made to function effectively. In these days an epidemic of typhoid fever or any other disease is a crime, and with all the scientific machinery now at our disposal it is inexcusable if more than a few days are required to find out the source of the epidemic. But I repeat, this Department could not interfere with provincial jurisdiction, and consequently the title "department of national health" is a misnomer. In the second place I object to the proposal to make the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment secondary to any other department of government as is being done here. When you associate it with this other department you are thinking of the enforcement of narcotic regulations and laws governing other offences and not of the real interests of the returned man. I believe also that it was promised, when the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment was formed, to keep it separate from any other department. In my opinion that department and its work should be independent of any other; nor should it be hidden under any other name. The department should be held prominently before all the people of the Dominion, and to make it an adjunct of a department of national health-to christen it at this late date a department of "veterans' welfare" -is to take a step in the wrong direction.
The work of soldier re-establishment has not diminished except to a very small degree. I do not know what departments are wiped out or are proposed to be wiped out by this bill, but I certainly think that this particular department should be kept prominently before the country. The mere fact that there is a special committee of the house to consider its affairs is sufficient pi'oof of its importance. I therefore again emphasize the desirability of keeping it independent of any other department. I should like to know who suggested that the affairs of the returned soldiers should not be considered by a special committee or that a special committee had not the time to deal with them. The members of the committee have not taken that stand. One man is as important to us as a dozen or a hundred; the case of one man is as worthy of consideration. I think it is a mistake to proceed with this resolution; I do not believe it is popular. Some little investigation held here -I rvish it had been under better auspices- may have been the reason for introducing this measure, but in my opinion the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment is important enough to give it precedence; nothing has been shown to warrant its being made secondary to any other department.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext: May I add to what the last speaker has said an expression of my own feeling to the same effect. If the minister woidd drop this resolution for the time being and let it stand on the order paper, considering the various changes that have been suggested, I think he would be doing a wise thing. "Veterans' Welfare" is not a propel name to give the department, and the men dc not want it. Why talk about veterans' welfare? They are not getting charity.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext: It is not intended as charity.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext: But the implication is there in the use of the word.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext: Not at all.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext:
Of course it is. And it is
an Americanism. Veterans' welfare, like community welfare, and other terms of that sort is an Americanism, and one that carries in the public mind implications which should be avoided in connection with the veterans and their affairs. I do not suggest another word, but I do suggest that the minister would be well advised to see whether he could not think of something more appropriate. Moreover, I do not think that an important department such as this, affecting so many men, women and children, should be tacked on to any other department. If you want to have two departments presided over by one minister, well and good. It would not make any difference in expense if the two were managed under one minister, but to amalgamate the two departments would be to do something which would be resented. The fact that they were tacked on as an adjunct to some other department would not meet with the approval of the veterans, who are entitled to feel that their affairs are administered by a department concerned! mainly with their interest. So far as the words "National Health" go, I do not know w7hat national health is. It is a wide term that might be applied to the people of Canada as a whole rather than to the people of any particular province or city. But if you were to speak of city health I do not know that anyone would understand you, unless perhaps you had in mind something having to do with drains or sewers or public undertakings of that sort. It is sufficient to have a "department of health"; you need not limit nor extend the term. Certainly you do not so by prefixing the word "national." If the minister would take the matter under advisement with a view to meeting some of the objections that have been advanced, I think it would be satisfactory for the moment.

speechtext: Why not? It is the same principle. That applies to all the departments, and I suggest that if the minister is sincere in his desire to pass this resolution, these words should be dropped. He should also justify the amalgamation of these two departments by showing that some economy will be effected and that greater efficiency will result.

speechtext: The question of the name is open for discussion, and as I said before it is my desire to secure a name which will be suitable and which will properly indicate the functions of these two departments. I wish now to establish the principle of amalgamation. In regard to economies, these will result very considerably in the work of administration. It is true that the estimates which have been tabled do not show these economies, because the estimates were made up prior to the work of reorganization and amalgamation. That will be made plain when the estimates come up, and possibly on the second reading of this bill.

Yes, if the house thinks it wise; as yet we do not know what the economies will be, because the reorganization is not complete. We know that a considerable saving will be made in our audit branch, but a reorganization of this character

National Health and Veterans' Welfare
takes a very considerable time. If it is the desire of the committee we might amend the resolution by striking out the words "National Health and Veterans' Welfare" for the present, and when the bill is in committee a name will be substituted which we trust will meet with the approval of members on both sides. I think we are all in agreement that if we accept the principle of amalgamation it is desirable to secure a name which will appeal to those interested in the work to be done.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext: I have every sympathy with any and every effort put forth by the Dominion of Canada to make the path of our returned soldiers easier, yet I think that the government should begin to see the importance of national health. During the greater part of my life I have been connected with public health work, and I claim that our country has not even a vision of what can be done by an aggressive, well conducted and well versed department of health. Canada to-day spends about 35 cents per capita on public health, while in order to have efficient service an expenditure of about $2.50 per capita is required. That simply shows the great gap between what we are endeavouring to do now and what might be done. I have been very much impressed by the remarks with regard to the recent epidemic in the city of Montreal. If the Dominion government had had a means of marshalling the forces of the country to grapple with that epidemic, the very serious situation which existed never would have come about. We should have a department of epidemiology. The infant mortality and maternal deaths in this country are simply startling; there is sufficient work in either of these branches of the work to call for aggressive action. I would prefer to see the Department of Health absolutely separate, to take over the matter of national health in line with what other countries are doing. I think there is sufficient work in this Dominion to keep that department busy if they would only buckle down to it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT
speechtext:
I am glad
the minister has agreed to leave out for the present the suggested name of this new department, because it does not ask us who vote for the legislation to commit ourselves to that name as would be the case otherwise. The objections which have been raised are very strong; at all events, they appeal to me as being such, but I am not prepared' to accept the idea of amalgamation, and I wish to express my opposition to that. From the standpoint of the amount of money which necessarily must be expended in looking after the soldiers of this country and from the stand-56103-122
point of the number of individuals directly or indirectly involved, which would include the women and children connected with returned or disabled soldiers, this department should stand alone. It should be a separate department with a minister and a deputy minister of its own. Under this proposed resolution the deputy will be deputy minister of Health and deputy minister of Veterans' Welfare. As far as the deputy minister of Health is concerned I do not think we could do better than the gentleman who occupies that position at present; he is certainly a very competent man, a medical man as you would naturally expect. I do not wish to place any limitation on his ability; probably he would efficiently fill the position of deputy minister of Militia or deputy minister of Veterans' Welfare, but it does seem to me that he will be more at home and more in his element while acting as deputy minister of Health than he would be in acting as deputy minister of Veterans' Welfare.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND VETERANS' WELFARE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF DEPARTMENTS OF HEALTH AND SOLDIERS' CIVIL KE-ESTABLISH-MENT

speechtext:
Does my hon.
friend know that the deputy minister has had very considerable war experience and military training?

speechtext:
That may be, but he is not going to live forever; I suppose he has no eternal lease on life, and I am discussing the principle now. I am not saying that the present deputy minister of Health might not make a competent deputy minister of Veterans' Welfare, but I do say that a man whose whole training has been along medical lines would be more in his element in directing the affairs of the Department of Health, while a man who has had experience along military lines or who had been closely identified with soldier problems would be more at home as deputy minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. If there are any individuals in the Dominion of Canada who are entitled to special consideration it is those who fought and were disabled in the war. I have no objection to the gentleman who occupies the position of Minister of Health also bearing the title of Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, but I do say there should be two distinct and separate departments, one dealing with soldier problems and one with health, each with a deputy minister. We owe that to the men who have sacrificed so much, and to their dependants,

who in many cases must be considered indirectly as wards of the nation. I merely wish to say that while the minister apparently thinks we should adopt the idea of amalgamation, I wish to express my opposition to the idea. I do not think it is a wise one. There should be two distinct departments, and there should be a deputy minister for soldiers' problems and a deputy minister of Health as well.

No, except that we will carry the work of pensions under the new amalgamation, as we do now. The general recommendations made by Mr. Scott- we cannot cover the situation fully unless we go more thoroughly into the report-are as follows:
(a) Giving to the Board of Pension Commissioners such staff as will enable them to function fully as an entirely separate body for the purpose of deciding upon the eligibility of pensioners and their dependants and calculating pensions payable.
And then he deals with transferring certain activities to the Department of Finance, and goes on to say:
(c)	All other activities now directed by the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment should be transferred to the Department of Health.
(d)	An official of the Department of Health should be appointed as secretary of the Board of Pension Commissioners.
Those are the recommendations which Mr. Scott made. In dealing with the affairs of the department, I think you will find he shows that the work is largely of the nature of treatment or health work, and the work of the vetcraft can be considered as a form of treatment; but on the whole that the amalgamation will be an advantage in the matter of administration, and also would lead to very considerable economy.
